title: Look at the thing
hook: look at the thing itself and do it steadily, kindly, modestly (Meditations 8.5)

segments.voice: Yesterday: not by reputation, the label set down and the quiet good done. Your line was not by reputation. What did you do that nobody will trace to you? Day five hundred ninety-seven.

A carpenter is fitting a door. The house is noisy, the client is hovering, his phone keeps buzzing, and there's a radio talking about the end of the world. None of it changes the door. The hinge still has to sit flush. The gap still has to be even. A good carpenter's eyes stay on the wood. Most of our days aren't like that. Our eyes are everywhere except the work in front of us. In book eight, Marcus Aurelius tells himself where to look.
screen: `A CARPENTER AND A DOOR.` → `NOISE EVERYWHERE.` → `EYES ON THE WOOD.`

segments.voice: First, clear the noise. Meditations eight, five, begins by telling Marcus not to be disturbed, because everything happens according to the nature of the whole, and in a little while he'll be nobody and nowhere, like the emperors Hadrian and Augustus before him. That's the radio switched off. Big worries put back to their actual size. Second, look. Then, he says, fix your eyes on the matter in front of you and look at it. Just that. See the actual task, not your feelings about it, not the story of how it'll go. Many of our struggles with work start because we never really look at the thing. We look at the dread around it. Third, remember the job underneath. While you look, keep in mind that your duty is to be a good human being, and do what human nature asks without turning aside. Fourth, the manner. Speak and act as seems most just to you, but do it with kindness, with modesty, and without pretense. Not just correctly. Kindly. Not just firmly. Modestly. Notice how calm that whole sequence is. Turn down the noise. Look at the thing. Remember who you're trying to be. Do it steadily and gently. That's not a heroic program. It's a carpenter's program. It works on a spreadsheet, a diaper, a hard email, a door. Whatever the thing is, it gets a little better when someone finally looks at it.
screen: `TURN DOWN THE NOISE.` · `FIX YOUR EYES ON THE MATTER.` · `REMEMBER: BE A GOOD HUMAN.` · `KINDLY, MODESTLY, NO PRETENSE.` · then, large: `STEADILY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one task waiting for you. Not the dread of it. The task itself. What exactly is it? What does the first step look like, physically? Where would your hands be? See it plainly, the way a carpenter sees the hinge. Then picture doing it slowly, steadily, kindly to anyone involved. Stay with the picture. The bell holds the time.
Look at the thing. Marcus's instruction to set the noise aside, look straight at the task, and do it steadily, kindly and modestly. Today's word.
Your line: steadily. Choose one task today, look right at it, and do it kindly and steadily, from first step to last. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use 8.5 as a short routine before difficult work: set aside big worries, look plainly at the task itself, and do it steadily and kindly.

trapdoor: what it means: quiet the big worries, see the task itself, and do it kindly as well as correctly.
what a scholar hears: 8.5 runs through three Stoic steps in miniature: physics (all follows nature), perception (see the thing as it is) and ethics (act justly, kindly, without pretense).

notes: Meditations 8.5 paraphrased: don't be disturbed, all is according to the nature of the universal; soon you'll be nobody and nowhere, like Hadrian and Augustus; fix your eyes on your business and look at it; remember your duty to be a good man; do what nature demands without turning aside; speak as seems most just, with good disposition, modesty and without hypocrisy. Confirm.
The three-step reading in the trapdoor follows Pierre Hadot's 'three disciplines'; interpretive, confirm framing.
